title: Robe (Kosode) with Spring Rice Fields
medium: Plain-weave silk crepe with resist-dyeing and hand-painting

altText: A Japanese silk robe whose fabric is covered by a dyed and painted design inspired by spring rice fields.

context: A kosode, the small-sleeved robe that developed into the modern kimono, made in Japan in the late 18th or first half of the 19th century. Its silk crepe is decorated with resist-dyeing and hand-painting, and the design takes spring rice fields as its theme.

descriptions.k: This is a robe from Japan. It is made of silk, and the whole cloth is a picture. The picture shows rice fields in spring. If you wore this robe, you would be wearing a landscape! What would you see if you looked closely?
descriptions.g12: This silk robe is called a kosode. It comes from Japan, and kimono grew from robes like it. The cloth is decorated like a picture of rice fields in spring. Artists dyed and painted the silk by hand. How is wearing a picture different from hanging it on a wall?
descriptions.g35: A kosode is a robe with small wrist openings, and it is the ancestor of the kimono. This one was made in Japan around 1800 and is decorated with a design of spring rice fields. Dyers used resist-dyeing, where something is applied to keep dye out of certain areas, and artists added hand-painting. Notice how the design covers the robe like a canvas. Why might someone want a robe that shows farm fields?
descriptions.g68: Kosode of the Edo period treat the robe as a large surface for design. Here the theme of spring rice fields turns a landscape into clothing, using resist-dyeing, in which patterns are protected from dye, plus hand-painting on silk crepe. The design must work when the robe is worn and moves, not only when it is laid flat in a museum. Look at how the pattern spreads across the surface. What might a farming scene mean to the person who chose it?
descriptions.g910: This kosode, from the late 18th or early 19th century, treats the robe as a canvas for a seasonal landscape. Rice-field imagery connects to the cycle of the year, which was a major theme in Japanese design and poetry. Resist-dyeing and hand-painting allowed a designer to build a pictorial composition on silk crepe. Consider how the image changes between a flat museum display and a moving body, and what choosing such a design might communicate about taste.
descriptions.g1112: As a kosode, this garment complicates the boundary between painting and dress. Spring rice fields give it a seasonal theme that fits wider Japanese traditions of tying design to time of year, while resist-dyeing and hand-painting show specialized textile craft. Museums usually display robes flat or on mounts, which differs from how they were meant to be seen, in motion on a body. Scholars also caution that the meanings individual patrons attached to a design often go unrecorded. How should we balance formal analysis with this uncertainty?

teacherNote.context: A silk kosode from the Edo period (late 18th to first half of the 19th century), made with resist-dyeing and hand-painting. The kosode is the forerunner of the modern kimono.
directions: Have students design a robe on paper with a theme from the seasons and explain how the pattern fits the shape of the garment.
Try a simple resist with wax crayon and watercolor wash so students can see how resist works.
Discuss the difference between seeing a garment flat in a museum and imagining it worn.
